judge:scholarly.top10_rationale:
I ranked candidates mainly by how severe the gap is in both Russian and English, by how unique and irreplaceable their information is, and by how many articles a first translation could support.

1. Hipparchus, Commentary on Aratus (item_119, score 9). It is the only surviving work of Hipparchus, it has no Russian or English translation, and it is the main witness to Eudoxus and Attalus.
2. Byzantine Alexander Poem (item_081, score 8). It has no translation in either language and sits at the centre of the editor's own field.
3. Zonaras I–VI (item_060, score 7). There is a gap in both languages, and its Alexander chapters show how Byzantine writers combined their sources.
4. Pollux 8 (item_065, score 7). It is a core lexicon of Athenian institutions and exists only in excerpts.
5. Scholia on Pindar's Pythians (item_106, score 7). They preserve fragments of lost Sicilian historians.
6. Scholia on Apollonius, Book 2 (item_108, score 7). Their Pontic ethnography and lost mythographers are of strong interest to Russian scholars.
7. Anonymous Theaetetus commentary (item_159, score 7). It is the earliest extant Platonic commentary.
8. Libanius' Letters (item_095, score 7). This large corpus could yield prosopography at the level of PLRE corrections.
9. Donatus on Terence (item_145, score 7). It has no Russian or English translation and is a key source for Roman stagecraft.
10. Next in line at score 6 are Quodvultdeus, Theon on the Almagest, the scholia on Aratus and Galen's De simplicium medicamentorum Book X. Each fills a gap where at least one language is missing.

Every candidate with a full Russian translation scored 1 or 2.

judge:readers.top10_rationale:
I scored only on reader appeal, launch value and fit with the name "Neoscholia". Statuses were taken as given; no new research was done.

The top three are ancient commentaries on texts readers already know. Iliad 6 scholia (item_107, 9) put Hector and Andromache beside the ancient scholia, so the platform's name explains itself. Scholia on the Clouds (item_114, 8) bring Socrates and comedy. Eustathius on Iliad 1 (item_110, 8) has the prestige of the major Byzantine commentary.

Servius on Aeneid 6 (item_144, 8) is the classic Latin scholiast on the underworld book, which is widely read. The Dodona oracle tablets (item_042, 8) are ordinary people's questions to Zeus: short, vivid, easy to share and new to Russian readers.

Pindar scholia on Pythian 1 (item_106, 7) and Apollonius scholia on the Black Sea peoples (item_108, 7) fit the "new scholia" idea closely. The second also has a strong Russian regional hook.

The remaining high scorers have strong names or news value. Cassius Dio books 1–35 (item_055, 7) cover early Rome by a major historian with no Russian translation. The Scythica Vindobonensia (item_058, 7) is a newly recovered historian on the Goths. The Byzantine Alexander Poem (item_081, 7) is translated nowhere and matches the editor's expertise.

Zenobius' proverbs (item_066), Aelian's animals (item_070) and Hipparchus (item_119) also scored 7, just outside the top ten. Every item with a full Russian translation got 1–2.

judge:feasibility.top10_rationale: Lens: feasibility and risk only. I tried to run checks, but the shared web-search budget was used up, so these scores rely on the statuses supplied with each candidate. Top 10: (1) item_055, Cassius Dio 1–35 (9): Greek prose, public-domain Boissevain text, the editor's own field, and the Russian status is high-confidence. (2) item_060, Zonaras I–VI (9): plain Byzantine prose with a public-domain text and an Alexander pilot. No Russian or English translation exists. (3) item_081, Byzantine Alexander Poem (8): public-domain Wagner text, the editor's specialty, and no Russian or English translation. The verse is easy to handle. (4) item_018, Quodvultdeus (8): Latin prose from PL 51 that the editor can check. (5) item_028, Cosmas and Damian miracles (8): simple Greek hagiography from public-domain Deubner. (6) item_066, Zenobius (8): short proverb entries and an easy pilot. (7) item_119, Hipparchus Book 1 (8): a CC BY-SA text in technical but regular Greek. (8) item_146, Porphyrio on the Ars poetica (8): short Latin scholia. (9) item_147, Ti. Claudius Donatus Book 4 (8): plain Latin with no Russian or English translation. (10) item_049, Abinnaeus petitions (7): short documentary Greek from the CC BY DDbDP. Low scores go to texts in cuneiform, Demotic, hieroglyphic or Ge'ez, which need outside reviewers and mostly have copyrighted editions. Fragmentary papyri with many gaps also score low. Every candidate with a full Russian translation got 1.
